answer: I'd like to talk about a fear that followed me for most of my life. A significant fear I managed to overcome was my long-standing fear of water, which had followed me since childhood, when I slipped into a pond and swallowed a lot of water before someone pulled me out. Growing up beside the Jamuna, not being able to swim was both limiting and slightly embarrassing. For years I avoided swimming entirely, and I would always find an excuse when my friends went to the river. Eventually, about two years ago, I decided enough was enough, and my cousin in the village, who is a strong swimmer, offered to teach me in the pond behind my grandparents' house. The first few sessions were genuinely [[terrifying]], and I nearly gave up several times. My cousin, however, was incredibly patient and encouraging, which made all the difference. Every weekend we travelled to the village, and he would stand beside me in the water, holding me up until I found my balance. Slowly but surely, my confidence began to grow, and I became less [[petrified]] of deep water. The moment I finally swam from one side of the pond to the other unaided was absolutely [[exhilarating]], and my grandfather clapped from the bank. Overcoming that fear gave me a huge sense of achievement that went far beyond swimming itself. Honestly, it taught me that most fears shrink once you [[confront them head-on]] rather than avoiding them. It was a genuinely [[empowering]] experience, and it made me braver about tackling other things I had been putting off out of fear.

followUps.answer: Not regularly, but whenever we visit my grandparents in summer, I go into the pond with my cousins. I am still not a strong swimmer, but I am no longer afraid, which is what matters.

followUps.q: Do you think children should learn to swim?
followUps.answer: Absolutely, especially in a country with so many rivers and ponds like Bangladesh. It is a basic safety skill, and it is much easier to learn as a child than as an adult.

note: Localised: fear rooted in a childhood pond incident, taught by a cousin in the grandparents' village pond instead of adult lessons; marked 'confront them head-on'.
